rows.stem: Though filariasis is not fatal, but the disease in humans is responsible for considerable suffering, gross deformities and disability. Write the scientific name of any two helminth worms causing the disease and state two chronic manifestations of filariasis.
"Curd is easier to digest by humans than milk." Justify, giving two suitable reasons.
rows.solution:
Curd is made from milk by **lactic acid bacteria (LAB)** such as Lactobacillus, which grow in milk and convert it to curd:
- The LAB **produce acids** (lactic acid) that **coagulate the milk** proteins.
- They also **partially digest the milk proteins**.

Since the proteins are already coagulated and partly broken down, curd is easier for humans to digest than milk. (Curd is also more nutritious, as the LAB increase its vitamin B12 content.)

rows.stem:
A person suffering from AIDS dies of opportunistic infections (ARC) i.e., infections that could have been otherwise overcome.
(i) State one reason as to why an 'HIV' patient dies of 'opportunistic infections'.
(ii) Give the scientific name of one bacterium and one parasite which mainly attack a person suffering from AIDS.
(iii) Write the full form of the name of the widely used diagnostic test for AIDS.
rows.solution:
(i) HIV infects and destroys the **helper T-lymphocytes**, so their number falls steadily and the person's **immunity is weakened**. The body can then no longer fight off infections it would normally overcome, and the person dies of these opportunistic infections.

(ii) A person with AIDS is mainly attacked by:
- the bacterium **Mycobacterium**;
- the parasite **Toxoplasma**.

(iii) The widely used diagnostic test is **ELISA: Enzyme Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay**. The marking scheme also accepts PCR, the Polymerase Chain Reaction.

rows.stem: In spite of the statutory warning on cigarette packets against 'smoking' and its injurious effects on health, smoking is still prevalent in the society. Enumerate four important health hazards to a smoker.

Study the given diagrams of Biogas plants – 'A' and 'B' and answer the questions that follow :
Which one of the two biogas plants can be used for generating gas fuel and electricity and why ? Give suitable reasons in support of your answer.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: two side-by-side drawings captioned Biogas Plant (A) and Biogas Plant (B), each an inlet box feeding a digester tank, with a gas holder and gas pipe on top and an outlet to a box marked Sludge. The two drawings differ only in the slurry label printed above the inlet box, which is the whole discriminator of the question, so which slurry feeds which plant is withheld here. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
**Biogas plant A**, the one fed with the slurry of dung.

Reasons:
- Biogas is produced by the **methanogens**, anaerobic bacteria such as Methanobacterium, and these are **present in the cow dung** (gobar), which is rich in them.
- In the digester they grow anaerobically on the cellulosic material of the dung and **produce large amounts of methane**, along with carbon dioxide and hydrogen.

This methane-rich gas is collected in the gas holder and supplied through the gas pipe, to be used as fuel for cooking and for generating electricity. The spent slurry is removed as sludge and used as a fertiliser.

rows.stem: Explain the two physiological attributes which enable a kangaroo rat to survive in desert conditions.
rows.solution:
The kangaroo rat of the North American deserts can meet all its water requirements without drinking water, through two physiological attributes:
- **Internal fat oxidation**: it oxidises its internal fat, and **water is formed as a by-product** of this metabolism, which meets its water needs.
- **Concentrated urine**: it can concentrate its urine, so that only a **minimal volume of water is used to remove excretory products**, and very little water is lost.

rows.subtopic: Species Numbers and Patterns of Biodiversity
rows.stem:
Study the given graphs (X) and (Y) depicting the annual variation in solar radiation on Earth from January to December and answer the undermentioned questions.
(i) Identify the graph that depicts (I) tropical region, and (II) temperate region, respectively.
(ii) Which of the two regions, (X) or (Y), will show high biological diversity and why ? Give two reasons.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: two graphs labelled (X) and (Y), each of Solar radiation (y, arrow upward) against Months from Jan. to Dec. (x, twelve ticks), each with a dashed horizontal reference line and one solid curve. The shape of each curve (how much the radiation varies over the year) is exactly what decides which graph is tropical and which temperate, so it is withheld here. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
In graph X the solar radiation changes a great deal through the year: it is low in January, rises above the dashed line around the middle of the year and falls low again by December. In graph Y it stays high and nearly constant, above the dashed line, all through the year.

(i) (I) The **tropical region is Y**, and (II) the **temperate region is X**. The marking scheme gives the half mark if either one or both of these are written correctly.

(ii) **Region Y**, the tropical region, will show high biological diversity, because:
- it is **less seasonal**, relatively more **constant and predictable**, which promotes niche specialisation and so a greater species diversity;
- it receives **more solar energy**, which contributes to higher productivity, and this in turn can support greater diversity, giving more scope for species diversification.

rows.stem:
(i) When prickly pear cactus was introduced into Australia in early 1920s, it caused havoc and ecosystem instability by achieving very high population densities. Explain the reason for its rapid spread into millions of hectares of rangeland.
(ii) State the importance of 'Prey-predator' relationship in a habitat.

When Plasmodium sp. (malarial parasite) enters the human body, it reproduces asexually and increases its number. During this course, the affected person suffers from malaria. After a number of asexual cycles, the parasite, in order to complete its life cycle, enters the sexual phase of its life. Trace the sexual stages in the life cycle of Plasmodium in a female Anopheles mosquito, when it bites an infected person, up to the formation of mature infective stages of the parasite.
rows.solution:
The sexual stages of Plasmodium in the female Anopheles mosquito:
- After the asexual cycles in the human, the parasite forms its **sexual stages, the gametocytes** (male and female), which **develop in the red blood cells**.
- When a female Anopheles mosquito bites the infected person, the **gametocytes are taken up with the blood meal**.
- **Fertilisation and development** take place in the **mosquito's gut**.
- The **mature infective stages (sporozoites)** are formed, **escape from the gut** and **migrate to the mosquito's salivary glands**.
- When this mosquito bites another human, the **sporozoites are injected with the bite**, and the infection is passed on.

The mosquito thus acts as the vector in which the sexual phase of the parasite is completed.

rows.stem:
(a) Name and state the type of immunity that acts as a 'biological shield' to the developing foetus against many infections in the mother's womb.
(b) A large proportion of infants remain free from potent infections at least three months after birth, or even longer if breast fed. Explain, giving suitable reasons.
rows.solution:
(a) The foetus is protected by **passive immunity**. This is the immunity in which **readymade antibodies are directly given** to protect the body against foreign agents, instead of the body producing its own. The foetus receives some antibodies from its mother **through the placenta** during pregnancy, and these act as its biological shield in the womb.

(b) Infants are protected because:
- the antibodies received from the mother during pregnancy continue to protect the baby for some time after birth;
- the yellowish fluid **colostrum**, secreted by the mother during the initial days of lactation, contains **abundant antibodies (IgA)** which protect the infant.

This is also passive immunity, so it lasts only a few months; continued breast feeding keeps supplying antibodies, which is why breast-fed infants stay protected for longer.

rows.stem: With the advent of sophisticated techniques of genetic engineering, we can now readily purify and isolate DNA. Name and explain the different steps involved in the separation and isolation of DNA fragments once cut by restriction endonucleases.
rows.solution:
The fragments are separated and isolated by **gel electrophoresis**:
- DNA fragments are **negatively charged** molecules, so in an electric field they **move towards the anode** (the positive electrode).
- They are forced through a matrix of **agarose gel**, a natural polymer extracted from sea weeds, which acts as a sieve.
- The fragments separate according to their size: the **smaller the fragment, the farther it moves**.
- The separated DNA fragments are made visible by **staining with ethidium bromide** followed by **exposure to UV radiation**; they appear as bright orange coloured bands. (Pure DNA cannot be seen in visible light without staining.)
- The bands are cut out from the agarose gel and the DNA is extracted from the gel pieces. This step is called **elution**.

The DNA fragments purified in this way are then used to construct recombinant DNA by joining them with cloning vectors.

rows.stem: "Some species in an ecosystem exert greater influence in driving major ecosystem services than others." How did Paul Ehrlich explain this concept in his 'rivet popper hypothesis' ?
rows.solution:
Paul Ehrlich explained it with an **analogy between an airplane and an ecosystem**:
- The airplane is the **ecosystem**, and all its parts are joined together using thousands of **rivets**, which are the **species**.
- If every passenger travelling in it starts popping a rivet to take home (a **species becoming extinct**), it may not affect flight safety (the **proper functioning of the ecosystem**) initially.
- But as more and more rivets are removed, the plane becomes **dangerously weak** over a period of time.
- Moreover, **which rivet is removed** also matters: the loss of rivets on the **wings**, which are the **key species that drive major ecosystem functions**, is a more serious threat to flight safety than the loss of a few rivets on the seats or windows inside the plane.

So some species exert greater influence on ecosystem services than others, and losing them harms the ecosystem most.

rows.stem:
(i) How has the introduction of Nile Perch into Lake Victoria in East Africa had a devastating effect on the indigenous species in the lake ?
(ii) Name two invasive weed species which have posed a threat to the existence of our native species.

Given below is a picture of a natural large habitat that is being continuously broken into smaller patches. This process is continuing, increasing and expanding over time due to human impact, thereby posing a great risk to the existence of species in the habitat.
(a) Do you agree with the above statement ? Give two suitable reasons in support of your answer.
(b) Write the ecological term used for such patches formed in an original habitat.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE: three sketched panels joined by arrows, from an 'Original Habitat' densely filled with trees, to a panel with fewer clumps of trees and 'Gaps', to a panel of isolated tree clumps with a label 'Gaps created over time due to human activities'; caption 'Habitat loss due to creation of 'patches' in a habitat'. The stem states everything the drawing shows, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
(a) **Yes**, I agree. Reasons:
- **Habitat loss and fragmentation** is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction. When a large habitat is broken up into small patches by human activities, the **habitat is degraded** and the species living there lose the space and resources they need.
- **Mammals and birds requiring large territories**, and certain animals with migratory habits, are **badly affected**, leading to a **decline in their populations**.

(b) Such patches are called **fragments**, and the process is **fragmentation** (habitat fragmentation).

rows.stem: An application of biotechnology in agriculture involves production of pest resistant plants using 'cry' genes from a bacterium. Name the bacterium. Explain why the 'cry' gene kills the pest but not the bacterium itself.
rows.solution:
The bacterium is **Bacillus thuringiensis** (Bt).

The 'cry' genes of Bt code for proteins (Bt toxin) that kill the insect pest but not the bacterium itself, because:
- In the bacterium, the toxin is formed as **protein crystals** that exist as an **inactive toxin (protoxin)**, so it does not harm the bacterium.
- When an insect ingests the inactive toxin, it is converted into the **active form** because the **alkaline pH of the insect's gut solubilises the crystals**.
- The activated toxin binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, which cause the cells to swell and lyse, **thereby killing the insect**.

rows.stem: Are two different types of restriction endonucleases used, one to cut the vector DNA and another to cut the desired DNA to be cloned ? Support your answer, giving reason.
rows.context: Development of recombinant DNA technology has opened gates to many breakthroughs in the fields of medicine and agriculture. This has enabled scientists to isolate, sequence and manipulate individual genes obtained from diverse living or dead cells. Given below is a diagram showing the basic steps involved in genetically modifying an organism. Study the given diagram and answer the questions that follow :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE: the case study's flow diagram: (1) Restriction Enzyme acting on a dark bar labelled (Gene of Interest) and (2) Restriction Enzyme acting on a ring labelled Plasmid (Vector); the two are bracketed and joined by an arrow marked (X) to (3) a ring with a dark insert labelled rDNA (vector); an arrow to (4) a cell labelled E. coli containing rings; four arrows to (5) four such cells, the group labelled (Y). This sub-part is answerable without it. Page idx 10.
rows.solution: **No.** The **same restriction endonuclease** is used to cut both the vector DNA and the desired DNA. Cutting both with the same enzyme gives DNA fragments with the **same kind of sticky ends**, which are **complementary** to each other, so the foreign DNA and the vector can be joined together end to end (by DNA ligase).

rows.context: Development of recombinant DNA technology has opened gates to many breakthroughs in the fields of medicine and agriculture. This has enabled scientists to isolate, sequence and manipulate individual genes obtained from diverse living or dead cells. Given below is a diagram showing the basic steps involved in genetically modifying an organism. Study the given diagram and answer the questions that follow :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: the case study's flow diagram, where the label (X) is defined: (X) marks the arrow that joins the restriction-cut gene of interest and the restriction-cut plasmid (vector) to give (3) rDNA (vector). Nothing is withheld; the stem also glosses the step. Page idx 10.
rows.solution: **DNA ligase.** It joins the cut foreign DNA (gene of interest) to the cut vector DNA at their complementary sticky ends, forming the recombinant DNA.

rows.stem: What is the term used for step (Y) showing multiple copies of the foreign DNA being formed in transformed E. coli ?
rows.context: Development of recombinant DNA technology has opened gates to many breakthroughs in the fields of medicine and agriculture. This has enabled scientists to isolate, sequence and manipulate individual genes obtained from diverse living or dead cells. Given below is a diagram showing the basic steps involved in genetically modifying an organism. Study the given diagram and answer the questions that follow :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: the case study's flow diagram, where the label (Y) is defined: (Y) marks the final group of four E. coli cells, each carrying several rDNA rings, reached by four arrows from the single transformed E. coli at (4). Nothing is withheld; the stem also glosses the step. Page idx 10.
rows.solution: The step is **cloning** (gene cloning, or host cloning): the transformed E. coli multiplies, and as it does, the recombinant DNA it carries is replicated, so multiple identical copies of the foreign DNA are formed.

rows.stem:
(i) What do you interpret from the bars (X and Z) obtained after 264 hours of treatment of monkeys with saline and \(2{\cdot}5\) mg/kg SiRNAs treatment ?
(ii) Name the category of organisms in the living world, where RNA interference (RNAi) takes place. Why ?
(iii) What is the basic principle involved in RNA interference (RNAi) in silencing the preferred genes ?
rows.context:
RNA interference (RNAi) holds great potential as a therapeutic agent for the treatment of human diseases and as a bicontrol agent for controlling pests in the agricultural fields. An experiment was conducted to study the use of 'RNAi' for the potential treatment of disorders of cholesterol metabolism. Some people possess genetic mutations with elevated levels of 'ApoB' gene which predisposes them to coronary artery diseases.

Lowering the amount of 'ApoB' can reduce the number of lipoproteins and lower the blood cholesterol.

Tracy Zimmerman and her colleagues used RNAi in 2006 to reduce the level of 'ApoB' in non-human primates Cynomolgus monkeys. (i) One group of monkeys were given RNAi treatment (Small interfering RNAs, SiRNAs) (doses 1 mg/kg SiRNAs), (ii) Second group of monkeys were given RNAi treatment (doses \(2{\cdot}5\) mg/kg SiRNAs), and (iii) Third group of monkeys were injected saline as control .

The results of the experiments are illustrated in the graph given below :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a bar graph of Relative serum cholesterol (% per dose) (y, 0 to 120 in steps of 20) against Time (hours) at 24, 48, 144 and 264 (x), with three bars at each time keyed Saline X (cross-hatched), 1 mg/kg Y (vertical wavy lines) and \(2{\cdot}5\) mg/kg Z (solid black). The bar heights, and so how X and Z change by 264 hours, are what part (i) asks the student to interpret, so they are withheld here. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(i) In the graph, the saline control bar X rises over time, from about 90 at 24 hours to about 112 at 264 hours, while the bar Z for the \(2{\cdot}5\) mg/kg SiRNAs falls, from about 65 at 24 hours to below 40 at 264 hours. So after 264 hours:
- in the saline-treated monkeys (X), the **cholesterol level increases**;
- in the monkeys given \(2{\cdot}5\) mg/kg SiRNAs (Z), the **cholesterol level decreases**.

This shows that the SiRNAs silenced the ApoB gene and lowered the blood cholesterol, and that the higher dose was effective, its effect growing with time.

(ii) RNA interference takes place in **all eukaryotic organisms**, because it is a **method of cellular defence**: the cell uses it to silence the RNA of invading viruses, and of transposons, that would otherwise be expressed.

(iii) The basic principle of RNAi is the **silencing of a specific mRNA** due to the **binding of a complementary double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)** molecule to it, which prevents the translation of that mRNA, so the preferred gene is not expressed.
